summary: Defines the 6top Protocol, which lets neighbor nodes in a 6TiSCH network add or delete Time-Slotted Channel Hopping cells with one another, enabling distributed scheduling. It is part of the 6top sublayer.

eli5.summary: Tiny sensors take turns talking at certain times and channels. This lets neighbors agree on which turns to give or take.

subtitle: How two neighboring nodes in a time-slotted wireless network negotiate which transmission slots to add, remove or move.

tldr.problem: In a 6TiSCH network every transmission is orchestrated by a schedule of cells. Nodes need a way to change that schedule together as traffic grows, shrinks or collides, without a central planner.
tldr.mechanism: 6P lets a node and one neighbor run a 6P Transaction of two or three steps (Request, Response, optional Confirmation) to add, delete or relocate cells, while a separate Scheduling Function decides when and which cells.
tldr.outcome: Both nodes end with matching schedules, and a sequence number detects when they have drifted apart. The rules for choosing cells are left to Scheduling Functions defined elsewhere.

facts.label: Commands
facts.value: 7 (ADD, DELETE, RELOCATE, COUNT, LIST, SIGNAL, CLEAR)

today: RFC 8480 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself defines no Scheduling Function and expects them to be defined in companion specifications.

sections.title: Why Neighbors Negotiate Cells
sections.content:
All communication in a 6TiSCH network is orchestrated by a schedule made of cells. Each cell is identified by a [slotOffset,channelOffset] pair. 6P, the 6top Protocol, lets a node ask a neighbor to add or delete Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) cells in the schedules of both nodes. The result is distributed schedule management.

The RFC describes three typical triggers, using node A (the one that sends a 6P Request) and node B (the one that receives it). If A sends more frames to B than its cells can carry, it asks to add cells. If it has more cells than it needs, it asks to delete some. If it sees collisions on a particular cell, it may ask to relocate that cell to a different [slotOffset,channelOffset].

6P itself does not decide when to do any of this. That is the job of a Scheduling Function, which the RFC leaves out of scope while specifying the requirements for one.
sections.eli5: Imagine two kids who share a walkie-talkie and a timetable of turns. When one needs more turns, gives some back, or finds a turn where someone keeps interrupting, they talk it over and both change their timetable the same way.

sections.title: 6top, Scheduling Functions and Cells
sections.content:
6top is the layer just above the IEEE Std 802.15.4 TSCH MAC layer. It has two roles: to terminate 6P, and to run one or more Scheduling Functions (SFs), which hold the rules that decide when to add or delete cells. A node MAY run several SFs at once, but at least one MUST be running. The SFID field in every 6P message tells the node which SF should handle a given transaction.

Cells are either hard or soft. A soft cell can be read, added, deleted or updated by 6top. A hard cell is read-only for 6top. All cells used by 6top in this specification are soft cells.

6P MAY be used alongside the minimal 6TiSCH configuration. In that case it is RECOMMENDED to use two slotframes: Slotframe 0 for the minimal configuration traffic, and Slotframe 1 for cells allocated by 6P. The minimal configuration slotframe SHOULD have higher priority, so dynamically allocated cells cannot mask its cells.
sections.eli5: The timetable has some fixed turns nobody may touch and some flexible turns that neighbors can swap. A helper called the Scheduling Function decides when a swap is a good idea, and 6P is how the swap gets agreed.

sections.title: 6P Transactions: Two Steps or Three
sections.content:
A 6P Transaction is a complete negotiation between two neighbors. It starts when a node wants to add, delete or relocate cells with a neighbor, and ends when the change has happened in both schedules or the transaction has failed. Both nodes must use the same SF for it to succeed. 6P messages SHOULD travel on dedicated (non-shared unicast) cells between the two nodes; if there are none, shared cells MAY be used.

In a 2-step transaction, node A picks the candidate cells. It locks them, sends a 6P ADD Request listing NumCells and a CellList with at least that many candidates, and starts a 6P Timeout once the request is link-layer acknowledged. Node B picks cells from the list, locks them and answers with a 6P Response naming the cells it chose.

In a 3-step transaction, node B picks the cells. Node A sends the request with an empty CellList, B replies with candidate cells, and A selects from those and sends a 6P Confirmation. An SF MUST say whether it uses 2-step transactions, 3-step transactions, or both.

Only one transaction at a time can run in a given direction between two neighbors. A node that receives a second request before answering the first MUST reply with RC_RESET.
sections.eli5: In the short version, one kid proposes a few times and the other picks. In the long version, the first kid asks for turns, the second suggests some, and the first picks from those, then says which ones. Either way, both write down the same turns.

sections.title: The 6P Message Format
sections.content:
6P messages travel over a single hop, carried as the payload of an 802.15.4 Payload Information Element (IE). They use a subtype of the IETF IE called the 6top IE, with subtype SUBID_6TOP. IEEE bit and byte ordering applies, so multi-octet fields are little endian.

Every message starts with the same fields: Version (only version 0 is defined), T (the message type: REQUEST, RESPONSE or CONFIRMATION), two reserved bits, Code, SFID and SeqNum. In a Request the Code field holds the command (such as ADD or DELETE); in a Response or Confirmation it holds a return code. The Request, Response and Confirmation of one transaction MUST share the same Version, SFID and SeqNum.

Commands that select cells carry a CellOptions bitmap with TX, RX and S (shared) bits, which map to the 802.15.4 link table fields. A CellList is a concatenation of 4-byte 6P Cells, each holding a slotOffset and a channelOffset. An SF MAY redefine the format of both CellOptions and CellList.
sections.eli5: Every note starts with the same little header saying what kind of note it is, who should handle it and which conversation it belongs to. After that come the details, like a list of the turns being talked about.

sections.title: The Seven Commands
sections.content:
The commands, in the order the RFC's registry lists them, are ADD (1), DELETE (2), RELOCATE (3), COUNT (4), LIST (5), SIGNAL (6) and CLEAR (7).

  • ADD adds cells. Node B reports back the cells it actually scheduled, which can be all of NumCells, none, or something in between. In every such case the return code is RC_SUCCESS.
  • DELETE removes cells that are already scheduled between the two nodes and match the CellOptions. If the CellList is empty, the receiving SF chooses the cells to delete.
  • RELOCATE moves cells to new locations. The request carries a Relocation CellList of exactly NumCells entries and a Candidate CellList. The SF SHOULD NOT relocate all cells between two nodes at once.
  • COUNT asks how many cells match given CellOptions.
  • LIST returns matching cells, starting at an Offset and up to MaxNumCells. The last answer carries RC_EOL, end of list.
  • SIGNAL carries opaque bytes between the SFs on the two nodes. Its use is defined by the SF.
  • CLEAR makes both nodes remove all cells scheduled between them. The SeqNum is not checked, and it is reset to 0 afterwards.
sections.eli5: Neighbors can add turns, give turns back, move a turn somewhere else, ask how many turns they share, ask for the list, pass a private note, or wipe the whole shared timetable and start over.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers, Timeouts and Errors
sections.content:
Each node remembers a SeqNum for each neighbor (and per SF). It starts at 0 after a node reset or a CLEAR, and is incremented by exactly 1 after every transaction. It is a lollipop counter: it rolls over from 0xFF to 0x01, never back to 0x00, so a value of 0 signals a reset neighbor.

The SeqNum has two jobs. It lets a node recognize duplicates: a message with the same SeqNum and type as the last frame from that neighbor must be link-layer acknowledged but silently ignored by 6top. It also detects a schedule inconsistency, for example when A has a transmit cell to B but B has no matching receive cell. That can happen after a power cycle or when the maximum number of link-layer retransmissions is reached. The detecting node answers with RC_ERR_SEQNUM, and the SF decides what happens next, for example a CLEAR, a LIST, or an internal rollback.

A node that sent a request but gets no Response within the 6P Timeout cancels the transaction. The SF chooses the timeout value. If a Response or Confirmation carries an error code, or a code the node does not recognize, the transaction is considered failed and no cells are added, deleted or relocated.
sections.eli5: Each pair of neighbors counts their conversations. If one suddenly forgets the count, for example after a power cut, the other notices the mismatch and they fix the timetable instead of listening on the wrong turns.

sections.title: What a Scheduling Function Must Define
sections.content:
Because 6P leaves the policy to SFs, the RFC lists what an SF specification has to cover. Each SF has a 1-byte identifier (SFID). The specification MUST give the rule for when to add or delete cells, how the source selects candidate cells and how the destination selects from them, the 6P Timeout, the rule for ordering cells, the meaning of the Metadata field, the node's behavior at boot, how to handle an inconsistency, what to do after an error, and the statistics to gather.

It SHOULD also state its application domain, include examples of normal and error cases, and define the SIGNAL payload. It MAY redefine the CellList and CellOptions formats. The RFC defines no SF itself, and the IANA registry of SF identifiers has no entries at the time of writing.
sections.eli5: 6P is only the way to talk. The rulebook for deciding what to ask for is a separate document, and this RFC lists the questions that rulebook must answer.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
6P messages MUST be secured through link-layer security, which is possible because they are carried as Payload IEs. Those IEs are encrypted and authenticated at the link layer with CCM*, and 6P defines no security mechanism of its own. It benefits from whatever key management the network uses.

6P does not protect against denial-of-service attacks, such as never sending the Confirmation in a 3-step transaction or sending badly formatted requests. Such cases SHOULD be handled by a policy like rate-limiting or time-limited blacklisting. The effect is mostly local to the two nodes involved, since they communicate in dedicated cells.
sections.eli5: The notes are locked in a box by the radio layer underneath, so strangers cannot read or fake them. But a neighbor who simply refuses to play fair can still waste your time, so you may need to ignore them.

messages.label: 6P ADD Request
messages.note: NumCells = 2, CellList = [(1,2),(2,2),(3,5)]. A locks the candidate cells.

messages.note: CellList = [(2,2),(3,5)]: the two cells B selected.

messages.label: L2 ACK
messages.note: Both schedules now contain the two cells.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Message type: REQUEST, RESPONSE or CONFIRMATION.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; SHOULD be zero and MUST be ignored on reception.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Command identifier in a Request, return code in a Response or Confirmation.

fields.name: SFID
fields.desc: Identifier of the Scheduling Function to handle the message.

fields.name: SeqNum
fields.desc: Matches the messages of a transaction and checks schedule consistency.
